People Skills
SHIPPED 2025 · 1.8M USERS
01 · CASE STUDY
AI that infers what employees are good at, across Microsoft 365.
PROBLEM
Profiles go stale. People fill them in by hand, then never touch them again.
SOLUTION
Skills inferred from work signals and kept current, with the person in control.
IMPACT
Shipped 2025. 1.8M users with AI-inferred skills on their profile.
WHAT WAS MINE
Led design for AI-inferred skills across Microsoft 365, Viva, and Copilot
Set the provenance pattern every surface reuses: where a skill came from, and how to correct it
Built the design system and the entire admin experience the product ships on
CHALLENGE
Skills grow.
Profiles don’t.
We fill in our skills by hand, or take the suggestions that come with our role.
Then we move on. New work, new tools, a new team. The profile doesn’t move with us. It waits until we want something.
So every skills system runs on stale data. And that data is how you find who can help, and how the company sees what it has.
MONTH 1 · YOU FILL IT IN
USERS
Employees, leaders, and admins wanted different things
Employees
Show what I’m good at without me maintaining a profile, and help me find the person who can help.
Leaders
Where are our skills, and where are the gaps? Across the org, not one person at a time.
Admins
Let me turn this on safely: who is included, what AI can infer, and what is visible.
HOW MIGHT WE
How might we keep every employee’s skills profile current without asking anyone to maintain it, and let each audience see only what it should?
EMPLOYEES
How might we surface skills people wouldn’t list, and let them decide who sees them?
LEADERS
How might we show where the org’s skills and gaps are without exposing any one person?
ADMINS
How might we make inferred data defensible enough to govern?
HYPOTHESIS
Give everyone a skills profile by default. Then make every skill accurate, transparent, and easy to correct.
If the profile is right without effort, people keep it. If a skill is wrong, they fix it instead of walking away. Three things had to be true, and they are the slides that follow.
Accurate
Ranked by the evidence behind each skill
Transparent
Every skill says where it came from
In the user’s control
Confirm, remove, hide; visibility on or off; admins set the floor
SOLUTION
Inferred once, shown in six places
PROCESS · ACCURATE, WITH DATA SCIENCE
How we decide which skills someone actually has
RESEARCH · RESPONSIBLE AI IN SKILLS
We asked people whether the inference felt fair.
People found the inferences fair. The AI only uses work signals.
The worry was misrepresentation: unverified skills, visible to everyone by default.
People liked that the inferences surfaced skills they would have forgotten to list.
People wanted more control: reorder, and finer visibility.
WHAT THE RESEARCH FOUND
“I want to be able to tell my own story.”

Measuring AI fluency
PROOF OF CONCEPT · NOT YET SHIPPED
02 · PROOF OF CONCEPT
Measuring how well people work with AI, from the work itself.
PROBLEM
Usage is countable. Whether people are getting better with AI is not.
PROPOSAL
Four capabilities staged from real work. One report for the person, one for the org.
STATUS
Research done, model running on real Copilot activity, reports prototyped.
WHAT IS MINE
Designed and ran the hero-scenario workshop across research, product, and design
Partnered with research on the phase-one user study
Defined the two-report model and specced it with product
CHALLENGE · WHY IT MATTERS
Companies count licenses and prompts. None of it says whether people are getting better.
AI fluency is knowing what to hand to AI, how to brief it, when to doubt it, and what you are still accountable for.
Access
Enablement and availability
Activation
A first successful outcome
Capability
Prompting confidence, task completion, AI fluency
Behavior
Repeat use across adjacent workflows
Outcome
Quality, capacity, velocity, risk reduction
COUNTABLE TODAY
WHERE AI FLUENCY IS THE EVIDENCE
THE RETURN ITSELF
RESEARCH · THE LEADER VIEW
Leaders are looking past adoption, and they told us why
From the senior-leader AI ROI research, the AI Workforce Think Tank, and the AI Fluency sessions with L&D and HR leaders. The think tank and the sessions still run monthly.
Capability. Strengths, gaps, change over time, and whether development is working.
Individual fluency tied to organizational readiness. Seen at scale, with access, governance, and leadership support in the picture.
Outcomes. Capacity, velocity, quality, and what became newly possible.
Something they can act on. Where a learning intervention is needed, and whether it worked.
Their employees do not know where they could use AI more effectively. So the report has to suggest what to try, as well as measure.
Leadership itself moves the outcome. Managers shape trust, experimentation, and critical thinking.
That is the report for learning and development leaders: getting better or not, where the gaps are, and what to do about them. The all-up org leader view is being shaped with the same think tank.
USERS · HOW MIGHT WE
How might we tell whether people are getting better at working with AI, from the work itself?
WHAT THE EMPLOYEE NEEDS
Am I getting better with AI, what is working, and what should I try next?
So: show someone where they stand and what to try next.
WHAT THE LEARNING LEADER NEEDS
Where are the gaps across my org, what behaviors drive them, and is the coaching working?
So: show leaders where the gaps are and what moves them, without ranking any one person.
PROCESS
A workshop to agree on what fluency looks like in real work.
Fluency shows up in behaviors, not in how much you use Copilot.
PROPOSED MODEL
Four capabilities, read from what people actually do
We observe behaviors, then group them into capabilities.
Twenty-four things people do with AI, pulled from real work
Delegation
What should AI do?
Recognizes where AI could contributeConsults AI on how to approach the problemRecognizes when work is not for AIConsiders AI’s strengths and limitationsStays actively involved in the workChooses an appropriate tool or approachAdjusts the division of work as the task evolves
Description
What does AI need to know?
Defines the intended audienceSpecifies the format and structureCommunicates the tone and styleBreaks complex work into stepsBuilds on previous exchangesProvides examples of what good looks likeDefines how AI should interactSets boundaries on what AI should and should not do
Discernment
Is AI’s work good enough?
Checks important facts and claimsNotices weaknesses in AI’s reasoningRecognizes missing contextEvaluates whether the collaboration is making progressRecognizes when AI’s communication is not working
Diligence
Am I using it responsibly?
Is careful about information shared with AIIs transparent about AI’s contributionTakes responsibility for AI-assisted workConsiders the consequences of sharing the work
PROCESS · SPECCED WITH DATA SCIENCE
Every stage traces back to something the person did
No stage is asserted. Each comes out of this chain, specced with data science, and every step keeps the evidence that produced it.

Build the pattern
Reliable, mixed or not yet
Coverage and spread

04 · EXPLAIN
Make it readable
The evidence behind it
What changed over time
Language a person can use
05 · ACTIVATE
Change the experience
A stage per capability
What to try next

RESEARCH · WE TOOK THE MODEL TO PEOPLE
We built the stages linear. Most of the twelve broke them.
EMERGING
DEVELOPING
CAPABLE
ADVANCED
Delegation
BEFORE
AFTER A NEW TOOL ARRIVED
Progression toward more capable use is real, but where someone is in it varies by tool, workflow, and scenario. A new tool moved experienced people back, without changing their stage.
Held. A stage per capability, never one score.
Changed. Progress does not require a stage change. People move forward and back within a stage without leaving it.
Ruled out. Reading fluency across every AI tool. The proof of concept stays on Copilot.
To test. Whether Emerging to Advanced matches how organizations already think: Aware, Assisted, Applied, Transformational.

OPEN QUESTIONS
What does it feel like to watch your own stage fall?
How much movement within a stage is meaningful, and how much is noise?
How does a compass stay a compass once leaders ask for a scorecard?
Do judgment behaviors count for more than routine ones?
Next: a study of the reports and the Copilot upskilling flows they lead to, where people can find them where they already work, and dedicated leadership feedback on the reports.
Both projects come back to the same question: what a system may claim about a person, how it shows its evidence, and how the person corrects it.
